messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jamal is a 22-year-old African American man who currently serves as a school principal. He has been in a relationship for several years and has sought help due to persistent distress related to childhood physical abuse by his caregiver. The traumatic memories have deeply affected him, particularly when triggered by old photos, unpredictable situations, or waking up from nightmares. Jamal's journey with PTSD began during his childhood when he endured repeated physical abuse at the hands of a caregiver. This trauma has left indelible marks on his psyche, manifesting in ways that disrupt his daily life and relationships. Old memories are often triggered by seemingly innocuous items such as old photographs, which serve as potent reminders of his painful past. When Jamal sees these photos, he finds it difficult to recall the events deliberately; instead, fragmented pieces of memory flood his mind in a disorienting manner. The vividness of these memories feels more real than ordinary recollections, making it challenging for him to differentiate between past and present. Jamal's negative appraisals are deeply intertwined with these triggers and memories. He harbors a profound fear that he will not be able to control his anger and might do something terrible as a result. This fear has led to a pervasive sense of helplessness, where Jamal feels unable to prevent bad things from happening to him. These feelings are exacerbated when he encounters unpredictable situations at work or home, which can instantly trigger distressing memories and reinforce his negative beliefs about himself. The cycle tightens when Jamal's memory difficulties fuel his negative appraisals. He struggles with recalling specific details of the traumatic events deliberately, yet the fragmented pieces that do surface feel overwhelmingly real. This inconsistency in memory reinforces his belief that he has permanently changed for the worse. These memories are often jarring and intrusive, leading to a cycle where each trigger intensifies his negative beliefs about himself. For instance, Jamal might be at work organizing a school event when an old photo from his childhood is displayed. The sudden appearance of this image triggers immediate distress. He finds himself struggling to recall the specifics of the abuse but feels overwhelmed by fragmented memories that seem more vivid and real than other recollections. This experience heightens his fear that he will lash out uncontrollably, exacerbating his feelings of helplessness and permanent damage. The cumulative impact of these experiences has taken a toll on Jamal’s daily functioning as a school principal. He has become increasingly withdrawn from social interactions and often avoids situations that might trigger unwanted memories. His relationship with his partner has also been strained, as he finds it difficult to open up about the intensity of his feelings and fears. Jamal's most recent episode was triggered when an unexpected situation arose at work, leading him to wake up from a nightmare feeling intensely distressed. This experience brought him to the brink, and he realized that these recurring patterns were not sustainable. The prospect of continuing in this cycle is both frightening and exhausting for Jamal. He seeks help with the hope of finding ways to manage his symptoms and regain control over his life. What frightens him most is the potential loss of control over his emotions and actions, but he also harbors a deep desire to heal and move past the shadows cast by his traumatic experiences.
